beats.success: Diego adds all four sides and orders the right amount of fence.
beats.redirect: The fence is too short, so Diego checks that he added all four sides and not only two.

beats.lead: Nia counts the squares inside the bed to order the soil.
beats.success: Nia writes the area in square units and orders the right number of soil bags.
beats.redirect: The unit does not make sense, so Nia draws one square unit and counts how many fit.

story.ending: The garden bed has a neat fence and plenty of soil, and Nia and Diego can say what area and perimeter each measure.

panels.says: Our bed is 6 feet long and 2 feet wide. I will add 6 + 2 + 6 + 2 to find how much soil we need.
That makes 16. But soil fills the inside, not the edge.
Oh. Adding the sides tells the distance around. What measures the inside?
Cover it with squares that are 1 foot on a side. There would be 2 rows of 6 squares.

predict.q: Before they count the squares, predict how much space the soil needs to cover.
options: 16 square feet
12 square feet
8 square feet
predict.why: There are 2 rows of 6 squares, so the area is 2 × 6 = 12 square feet.

transfer.relationship: The inside of a rectangle is covered by equal rows of unit squares, and the number of squares is its area
phrasings: 3 rows of 5 one-foot squares cover the bed
5 × 3 = 15 square feet
The bed is 5 feet long and 3 feet wide, so its area is 15 square feet
A model with 5 columns and 3 rows of unit squares

decoys.why: This adds the sides, so it finds the perimeter, not the space inside.

decoys.text: The bed needs 15 feet of fence
decoys.why: Fence goes around the edge and is measured in feet, but 15 is a count of squares inside the bed.

modeling.title: Planning a garden bed
modeling.scenario: A fictional class plans a rectangular garden bed. They need fence along the edge and soil to cover the inside. All the numbers are invented for the exercise.

given.label: Space one bag of soil covers

assumptions: The bed is a perfect rectangle.
Every square foot gets the same layer of soil.
The fence goes right along the edge with no gaps.
prompts: How much fence goes around the bed?
What is the area of the bed in square feet?
How many bags of soil does the class need if each bag covers 6 square feet?
limits: Real garden beds have corners that are not exactly square.
A real fence needs a gate, so the amount of fence might change.

sentence.base: The garden bed has an area of 15 square feet.
sentence.because: The garden bed has an area of 15 square feet because 3 rows of 5 square units cover it.
sentence.but: The garden bed has an area of 15 square feet, but its perimeter is 16 feet.
sentence.so: The bed is covered by 3 rows of 5 squares, so its area is 15 square feet.

diagnostic.prompt: Draw a rectangle that is 4 units long and 3 units wide. Find its area and its perimeter, and tell what each number measures.
lookFor: Covers the rectangle with 3 rows of 4 squares and writes 12 square units
Adds all four sides to get 14 units
Says that area is the space inside and perimeter is the distance around
diagnostic.language: Let the student trace the edge with a finger and then sweep a hand across the inside before writing. If the numbers are right, the barrier is the words area and perimeter, not the measuring.

extension.task: Find two different rectangles that each have an area of 16 square units. Find the perimeter of each one.
extension.reasoning: Explain why rectangles with the same area can have different perimeters.

en.learning: Your child is learning the difference between area, the space inside a shape, and perimeter, the distance around it.
en.say: Say "area is the inside and perimeter is the edge." Use square units for area and plain units, like feet, for perimeter.
en.ask: A rug is 4 feet long and 3 feet wide. How long is the edge all the way around?
en.activity: Walk around the edge of a table and measure each side with a ruler. Then cover the top with square sticky notes and count them to find the area.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo la diferencia entre el área, que es el espacio dentro de una figura, y el perímetro, que es la distancia alrededor.
es.say: Digan "el área es el interior y el perímetro es el borde". Usen unidades cuadradas para el área y unidades simples, como pies, para el perímetro.
es.ask: Una alfombra mide 4 pies de largo y 3 pies de ancho. ¿Cuánto mide todo el borde alrededor?
es.activity: Caminen alrededor del borde de una mesa y midan cada lado con una regla. Después cubran la superficie con notas adhesivas cuadradas y cuéntenlas para hallar el área.

skills.objective: Students tell and write time to the nearest minute on an analog clock and solve elapsed time problems by jumping forward on a number line, adding the parts of the interval.
skills.studentObjective: I can read a clock to the minute and find how much time passes from a start time to an end time.
skills.languageObjective: I will explain how I found the elapsed time using because, but and so with the words elapsed time, minute, hour and past.
successCriteria: I read the hour hand and the minute hand and write the time to the minute.
I remember that each number on the clock stands for 5 minutes.
I find elapsed time by jumping to the next hour and adding the parts.
I write the unit, minutes or hours, with my answer.
skills.bigIdea: Elapsed time is how much time passes from a start time to an end time, and it can be found by jumping forward on a number line in friendly steps and adding them.

syntax: The activity starts at ___ and ends at ___, so ___ minutes pass.
It is ___ minutes past ___ because the minute hand points to ___.
discourse: Tell what happens from a start time to an end time in order
Explain how jumps on a number line add up to the elapsed time

domains.listening: Students listen to a description of a practice and tell the start time, the end time and how long it lasted.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner the time to the minute and describe their jumps on a number line.
domains.reading: Students read a short passage and underline each time and each length of time.
domains.writing: Students write a sentence that tells how much time passed and how they know.

vocab.def: The amount of time that passes from a start time to an end time.
vocab.example: From 2:40 to 3:15 the elapsed time is 35 minutes.
vocab.nonExample: The end time 3:15 by itself
vocab.sentence: Tariq finds the elapsed time for the walk.

vocab.def: A unit of time. There are 60 minutes in one hour.
vocab.example: A song that lasts 3 minutes
vocab.nonExample: A day, which is much longer than a minute
vocab.sentence: The walk takes 35 minutes.
vocab.everyday: Very small, as in a minute amount of dust; said like my-NOOT

vocab.def: A unit of time that is 60 minutes long.
vocab.example: A class that lasts 1 hour is 60 minutes.
vocab.nonExample: A second, which is much shorter
vocab.sentence: One hour has 60 minutes.

vocab.def: After a given hour, when we tell time by counting minutes.
vocab.example: 3:15 is 15 minutes past 3.
vocab.nonExample: A quarter to 4, which is before the hour
vocab.sentence: The hour hand is just past the 3.
vocab.everyday: Something that already happened, as in the past

vocab.def: The long hand on a clock that shows how many minutes after the hour.
vocab.example: At 2:35 the minute hand points to the 7.
vocab.nonExample: The short hand, which is the hour hand
vocab.sentence: The minute hand moves around the clock face once in an hour.

misconceptions.belief: The number the minute hand points to is the number of minutes.
misconceptions.why: Students read the clock numerals like a number line from 1 to 12 and forget that each number stands for a group of 5 minutes.
misconceptions.fix: Count around the clock by fives while pointing at each number, and write the minutes next to each numeral until students remember them.

errorCase.story: A clock has the hour hand between the 2 and the 3, and the minute hand on the 7.
steps: The hour hand is between the 2 and the 3, so the hour is 2.
The minute hand is on the 7, so the time is 2:07.
errorCase.explain: Each number on the clock stands for 5 minutes. The 7 means 7 × 5 = 35 minutes, so the time is 2:35.

misconceptions.belief: To find elapsed time, subtract the hours and then subtract the smaller minutes from the larger minutes.
misconceptions.why: Students treat the clock times like two whole numbers and turn the subtraction around when the minutes will not take away.
misconceptions.fix: Draw a number line and jump from the start time to the next hour, then to the end time, and add the jumps.

errorCase.story: Practice starts at 3:50 and ends at 4:20.
steps: The practice starts at 3:50 and ends at 4:20.
I subtract the hours and the minutes: 4 − 3 = 1 hour and 50 − 20 = 30 minutes.
So the elapsed time is 1 hour 30 minutes.
errorCase.explain: You cannot take 50 minutes away from 20 minutes. Jump instead: 3:50 to 4:00 is 10 minutes, and 4:00 to 4:20 is 20 minutes more. The elapsed time is 30 minutes.

misconceptions.belief: There are 100 minutes in one hour.
misconceptions.why: Students are used to counting in tens and hundreds, and they carry that pattern over to the clock.
misconceptions.fix: Count around a clock by fives to 60 and make a hands-on chart of 60 minutes in 1 hour.

errorCase.story: Practice lasts 45 minutes and then games last 30 minutes.
steps: 45 + 30 = 75 minutes.
An hour is 100 minutes, so 75 minutes is less than 1 hour.
errorCase.explain: An hour is 60 minutes, not 100. 75 minutes is 60 minutes and 15 more, so it is 1 hour and 15 minutes.

misconceptions.belief: The word minute always means the unit of time on a clock.
misconceptions.why: The spelling is the same for the unit of time and for the word that means tiny, but the pronunciation and the meaning change.
misconceptions.fix: Say each word aloud with a picture: MIN-it for the unit on a clock and my-NOOT for a tiny speck. Ask which one the problem uses.

reading.title: The Walk to the Library
reading.text: Mei-Lin and Tariq walk to the library after school. They leave at 2:40, and they arrive at 3:15. Tariq wants to find the elapsed time, which is how much time passes from the start to the end. He draws a number line. From 2:40 to 3 o'clock is 20 minutes, and from 3 o'clock to 3:15 is 15 minutes more. He adds 20 + 15 = 35, so the walk takes 35 minutes. At the library, the minute hand points to the 3, and the hour hand is just past the 3. Each number on the clock stands for 5 minutes, so the clock shows 3:15. One hour has 60 minutes, so the walk was less than an hour.
reading.simple: Mei-Lin and Tariq walk to the library. They leave at 2:40. They arrive at 3:15. Tariq finds the elapsed time. He uses a number line. From 2:40 to 3 o'clock is 20 minutes. From 3 o'clock to 3:15 is 15 minutes more. 20 + 15 = 35, so the walk takes 35 minutes. At the library, the minute hand points to the 3. The hour hand is just past the 3. Each number on the clock stands for 5 minutes. One hour has 60 minutes.

questions.q: What time do Mei-Lin and Tariq arrive at the library?
Why does Tariq stop at 3 o'clock on his number line?
questions.a: Jumping to the next hour gives a friendly jump of 20 minutes, and then he only has 15 minutes left to add.

questions.q: The walk takes 35 minutes. Is that more or less than an hour, and how do you know?
questions.a: Less than an hour, because 1 hour is 60 minutes and 35 is less than 60.

wdntb.why: The first three describe the 35 minutes of the walk, but 3:15 to 2:40 goes backward in time.

noticeWonder.prompt: Look at a number line with 2:40 on the left, 3 o'clock in the middle and 3:15 on the right. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: The elapsed time from 2:40 to 3:15 is the same as the elapsed time from 4:40 to 5:15.
asn.why: Both start 20 minutes before the hour and end 15 minutes after the next hour, so both are 35 minutes.

asn.claim: An activity that starts in the morning also ends in the morning.
asn.why: An activity from 9:30 a.m. to 10:15 a.m. stays in the morning, but one from 11:40 a.m. to 12:10 p.m. ends after noon.

wyr.q: Would you rather find elapsed time by jumping on a number line or by counting on a clock face?

compare.a: Amina jumps on a number line from 4:10 to 4:30, then to 4:45: 20 minutes plus 15 minutes.
compare.b: Beto counts by fives on the clock face from 4:10 to 4:45: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35.
compare.prompt: Do both ways give the same elapsed time? Which way is easier to check, and why?

debate.claim: It is easier to find elapsed time when you jump to the next hour first.
debate.forEvidence: Jumping to the hour makes friendly steps, like 2:40 to 3 o'clock is 20 minutes, and then you add the rest.
debate.againstEvidence: Some times, like 2:10 to 2:25, are inside the same hour, so jumping to the next hour is extra work.

listening.script: Listen to Tariq explain his soccer practice. Practice starts at 4:10 and ends at 4:55. I jump from 4:10 to 4:30, which is 20 minutes. Then I jump from 4:30 to 4:55, which is 25 minutes. I add 20 plus 25, so the elapsed time is 45 minutes. My teammate says it is 55 minutes, because the end time has a 55 in it. But the 55 only tells where the minute hand points. It does not tell how much time passed.

tasks.q: How long is Tariq's soccer practice?
options: 20 minutes
25 minutes
45 minutes
55 minutes
tasks.why: Tariq adds the jumps 20 minutes and 25 minutes to get 45 minutes.

tasks.q: Tariq's teammate says practice is 55 minutes long. What is the mistake?
options: He used the end time as the elapsed time.
He added 20 and 25 wrong.
He forgot that an hour has 60 minutes.
tasks.why: The 55 in 4:55 tells where the end is, not how much time passed from the start.

story.title: The Museum Trip
story.setting: the school bus on a field trip day
story.goal: get the class to the science museum and back on schedule
story.intro: Mei-Lin is the class timekeeper for a trip to the science museum. Her teacher asks her to keep track of when each part of the day starts and ends so that the bus can leave on time.

beats.lead: Mei-Lin writes the time the bus leaves and looks at the clock at the museum doors.
beats.success: She reads the clock to the minute and writes the time correctly on her chart.
beats.redirect: The time she wrote looks too early, so she counts by fives around the clock face to check.

beats.lead: Tariq asks how long the bus ride took from the school to the museum.
beats.success: They jump on a number line from the start time to the end time and find the elapsed time.
beats.redirect: The elapsed time does not fit the clock, so they draw jumps to the next hour and add them.

beats.lead: The teacher asks the class to plan when the group should leave the museum.
beats.success: Mei-Lin adds the length of each activity to the start time and writes a clear schedule.
beats.redirect: The schedule runs past the bus time, so Mei-Lin checks each jump again.

story.ending: The bus leaves on time, and Mei-Lin can explain how she found each elapsed time.

panels.says: The bus leaves at 1:20 and gets to the museum at 2:05.
So I subtract the minutes: 20 minus 5 is 15 minutes.
Hmm. Let us jump on a number line from 1:20 to 2 o'clock first.
Oh! That jump is 40 minutes, and then there are 5 more minutes to reach 2:05.

predict.q: Before they finish the jumps, predict the elapsed time of the bus ride.
options: 15 minutes
45 minutes
85 minutes
predict.why: From 1:20 to 2 o'clock is 40 minutes, and 5 more minutes reaches 2:05, so 40 + 5 = 45 minutes.

transfer.relationship: Elapsed time is the time that passes from a start time to an end time, found by jumping forward and adding the jumps
phrasings: The walk starts at 2:40 and ends at 3:15
From 2:40 to 3:15 is 20 minutes plus 15 minutes
A number line with a jump of 20 minutes and a jump of 15 minutes
35 minutes pass between 2:40 and 3:15

decoys.text: The walk takes 15 minutes because it ends at 3:15
decoys.why: The end time is a place on the clock. It does not tell how much time passed from the start.
Adding two clock times does not tell how much time passed. Elapsed time comes from jumping forward from the start.

modeling.title: Planning a field trip day
modeling.scenario: A fictional class plans a trip to a nature center. The bus ride and each activity have a set length of time. All the times are invented for the exercise.
assumptions: The bus leaves exactly on time.
Each activity starts as soon as the one before it ends.
The whole class arrives at the same moment.
prompts: What time does the bus arrive at the nature center?
If the nature walk starts right when the bus arrives, what time does it end?
Lunch follows the walk. What time does lunch end, and how many minutes has the class been at the center?
limits: Real buses can be delayed by traffic, so the arrival time could change.
Real groups need a few minutes to move between activities.

sentence.base: The elapsed time from 2:40 to 3:15 is 35 minutes.
sentence.because: The elapsed time from 2:40 to 3:15 is 35 minutes because 20 minutes plus 15 more minutes makes 35 minutes.
sentence.but: The walk ends at 3:15, but the elapsed time is 35 minutes, not 15 minutes.
sentence.so: From 2:40 to 3 o'clock is 20 minutes and 15 minutes more is added, so the elapsed time is 35 minutes.

diagnostic.prompt: A game starts at 3:35 and ends at 4:10. Show the elapsed time on a number line and explain how you found it.
lookFor: Jumps to the next hour and writes 25 minutes
Adds the last jump of 10 minutes
Writes 35 minutes and includes the unit
diagnostic.language: Let the student point to the start and end on a drawn number line and show the jumps before speaking or writing. If the jumps are right, the barrier is the time vocabulary, not the thinking.

extension.task: A movie starts at 1:50 and lasts 1 hour and 25 minutes. Find the end time and show your jumps on a number line.
extension.reasoning: Explain why you cannot find the end time by adding 1:50 and 1:25 like ordinary numbers.

en.learning: Your child is learning to tell time to the minute and to find how much time passes between a start time and an end time.
en.say: Say the time two ways, like "2:40, or twenty minutes before three." Count by fives around the clock.
en.ask: If we leave at 4:15 and the trip takes 30 minutes, when do we arrive?
en.activity: Pick an event from your day, like dinner or the bus ride. Write the start and end times and ask your child to show the elapsed time with jumps on a drawn number line.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo a decir la hora al minuto y a hallar cuánto tiempo pasa entre una hora de inicio y una hora final.
es.say: Digan la hora de dos maneras, como "las 2:40, o tres menos veinte". Cuenten de cinco en cinco alrededor del reloj.
es.ask: Si salimos a las 4:15 y el viaje dura 30 minutos, ¿a qué hora llegamos?
es.activity: Elijan una actividad del día, como la cena o el camino a la escuela. Escriban la hora de inicio y la hora final, y pidan a su hijo o hija que muestre el tiempo transcurrido con saltos en una recta numérica dibujada.

skills.objective: Students solve two-step word problems with whole numbers by writing equations with a letter for the unknown, checking that the equation matches the story, and judging whether the answer is reasonable.
skills.studentObjective: I can write an equation with a letter for the unknown in a two-step story, solve it, and check that my answer makes sense.
skills.languageObjective: I will explain how my equation matches a story using because, but and so with the words equation, unknown, two-step problem and reasonable.
successCriteria: I tell what happens in each step of a story and what I do not know yet.
I write an equation with a letter that matches the story.
I solve the steps in an order that fits the story.
I check the answer with an estimate or by working backward.
skills.bigIdea: An equation is a model of what happens in a story, so the order of the steps in the story decides the order of the operations.

syntax: First I find ___ because ___, and then I ___.
The letter ___ stands for the number of ___ that we do not know.
discourse: Retell a story in the order things happen
Justify why an equation matches a story and why an answer is reasonable

domains.listening: Students listen to a booth story and tell what happens first and what happens next.
domains.speaking: Students retell a story to a partner, naming what is known and what is unknown before they choose operations.
domains.reading: Students read a short passage and mark each number with what it counts.
domains.writing: Students write an equation with a letter and a sentence that explains why the equation fits the story.

vocab.def: A math sentence with an equal sign that says two amounts are the same.
vocab.nonExample: 5 × 8, which has no equal sign
vocab.sentence: Fatima writes an equation to show what happens in the story.

vocab.def: A number you do not know yet, shown with a letter or a box.
vocab.example: In 40 − 13 = n, the unknown is n.
vocab.nonExample: The number 40, which the story tells us
vocab.sentence: The letter n is the unknown number of beads.

vocab.def: A problem that needs two operations, one after the other, to find the answer.
vocab.example: Find the total in 5 bags of 8, then take away 13.
vocab.nonExample: Find the total in 5 bags of 8, and stop
vocab.sentence: The bead story is a two-step problem.

vocab.def: Makes sense when you compare it with a rough guess or with the story.
vocab.example: 27 is reasonable because 40 take away about 10 is about 30.
vocab.nonExample: An answer of 53, which is more than the 40 beads at the start
vocab.sentence: Fatima asks whether the answer is reasonable.
vocab.morphology: reason means a way of thinking; -able means able to be

vocab.def: In a subtraction story, what remains after some are taken away.
vocab.example: 40 beads, 13 used, and 27 left on the table
vocab.nonExample: The left side of the table
vocab.sentence: There are 27 beads left after the bracelets are made.
vocab.everyday: The opposite of right, or a direction that points to the side where your left hand is

misconceptions.belief: In a story with groups and a take-away, subtract from the number in one group first.
misconceptions.why: Students pair the numbers that are close together in the sentence instead of asking what the amount taken away comes out of.
misconceptions.fix: Draw the story as a picture. Ask what the stickers given away come from, one pack or all the packs together, and do that step first.

errorCase.story: Joaquín has 4 packs with 6 stickers in each pack and gives away 5 stickers.
steps: There are 4 packs with 6 stickers each, and 5 stickers are given away.
I subtract first: 6 − 5 = 1.
Then 4 × 1 = 4 stickers are left.
errorCase.explain: The 5 stickers come out of the total, not out of one pack. Find the total first: 4 × 6 = 24. Then subtract: 24 − 5 = 19 stickers left.

misconceptions.belief: In n + 8 = 20, add 8 and 20 to find the unknown.
misconceptions.why: Students see a plus sign and apply it to the numbers they can see, instead of asking what number joins 8 to make 20.
misconceptions.fix: Draw a tape diagram with a whole of 20 and a part of 8. Ask what the missing part is, then check by adding it to 8.

errorCase.story: Fatima writes n + 8 = 20 for a story about a bag of beads and 8 more beads that make 20 in all.
steps: The equation is n + 8 = 20.
I add 8 and 20: n = 28.
errorCase.explain: The total is 20, and n is a part. The missing part is 20 − 8 = 12, and 12 + 8 = 20 checks it.

misconceptions.belief: Any equation that uses all the numbers in the story fits the story.
misconceptions.why: Students collect the numbers from a story and connect them with operations without picturing what happens to the amounts.
misconceptions.fix: Retell the story with objects. Decide which amounts are groups and which amount joins the total, then write the equation in the same order.

errorCase.story: A shelf has 3 rows with 8 books in each row. Then 2 more books are put on the shelf.
steps: The shelf has 3 rows of 8 books, and 2 books are put on it.
I write 3 × 8 × 2 = n.
errorCase.explain: The 2 books join the 24 books that are already there. They are not another group of the same size. Write 3 × 8 + 2 = n, so n = 26 books.

misconceptions.belief: How many are left asks about the left side.
misconceptions.why: Left is a direction word in many lessons, so the meaning of what remains is easy to miss in a question.
misconceptions.fix: Act out a story with counters: take some away and say what remains. Ask whether the word points to a place or to an amount.

reading.title: The Bead Booth
reading.text: Fatima and Joaquín run a bead booth at the school fair. They buy 5 bags of beads, and each bag holds 8 beads. They write the equation 5 × 8 = 40 to find the total number of beads. Then children make bracelets, and the booth uses 13 beads. This is a two-step problem, because they multiply first and then subtract. Joaquín writes 40 − 13 = n. The letter n is the unknown, a number they do not know yet. He finds that n is 27. Fatima asks whether the answer is reasonable. She thinks that 40 take away about 10 is about 30, so 27 makes sense. There are 27 beads left on the table.
reading.simple: Fatima and Joaquín run a bead booth at a fair. They buy 5 bags of beads. Each bag holds 8 beads. They write the equation 5 × 8 = 40 to find the total. Children make bracelets, and the booth uses 13 beads. This is a two-step problem. Joaquín writes 40 − 13 = n. The letter n is the unknown. He finds that n is 27. Fatima checks if the answer is reasonable. She thinks 40 take away about 10 is about 30, so 27 makes sense. There are 27 beads left.

questions.q: How many beads are in each bag?
questions.a: 8 beads

questions.q: Why do Fatima and Joaquín multiply before they subtract?
questions.a: The 13 beads that are used come out of all 40 beads, so they have to find the total first.

questions.q: How does the estimate 40 − 10 = 30 show that 27 is reasonable?
questions.a: The beads used, 13, are a little more than 10, so the answer should be a little less than 30. 27 is a little less than 30.

wdntb.why: The first three describe parts of the same story, but 40 + 13 adds beads that the booth used up.

noticeWonder.prompt: Look at a tape diagram that shows 5 equal groups of 8 with a piece of 13 taken away. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: The letter in an equation can stand for a number that we do not know yet.
asn.why: A letter or a box in an equation holds the place of the unknown number.

asn.claim: You need two separate equations to solve a two-step problem.
asn.why: You can write two equations, 5 × 8 = 40 and 40 − 13 = n, or one equation, 5 × 8 − 13 = n.

wyr.q: Would you rather write one equation for the whole story or two short equations, one for each step?
wyr.a: One equation for the whole story
wyr.b: Two short equations, one for each step

compare.b: Leo writes 8 − 13 = k and then 5 × k = n.
compare.prompt: Which plan matches the bead story? What goes wrong in the other plan?

debate.claim: You do not need an estimate if you already have an exact answer.
debate.forEvidence: The exact answer, 27, is a number that you worked out, so it must be right.
debate.againstEvidence: An estimate like about 30 shows whether an exact answer is reasonable, and it can catch a mistake.

listening.script: Listen to Joaquín tell about the bead booth. We bought 6 bags with 5 beads in each bag. That is 6 times 5, which is 30 beads. Then we used 9 beads for necklaces. I write 30 minus 9 equals n. The n is the unknown, because I do not know the beads left yet. My friend says to subtract 9 from 5 first. But the 9 beads came out of all 30 beads, not out of one bag. So first I find the total, and second I take away. There are 21 beads left.

tasks.q: How many beads are left at the booth?
tasks.why: Joaquín finds 6 × 5 = 30 beads, and then 30 − 9 = 21 beads.

tasks.q: Joaquín's friend wants to subtract 9 from 5 first. What is wrong with that plan?
options: The 9 beads came out of all 30 beads, not out of one bag.
Nine is too large a number to subtract.
Subtraction must never come last.
tasks.why: The beads used come out of the whole total, so the total must be found first.

story.title: The Bracelet Booth
story.goal: run the bead booth so every bracelet has enough beads
story.intro: Fatima and Joaquín have a table at the school fair with boxes of beads, string and a sign. Children line up to make bracelets, and Fatima keeps a notebook to track the beads.

beats.lead: Fatima reads the supply list and decides what she knows and what she does not know yet.
beats.success: She tells the story in order and writes an equation with a letter for the unknown.
beats.redirect: The equation does not match the story, so Fatima retells it step by step with counters.

beats.lead: Joaquín solves the first step and then the second step of the supply problem.
beats.success: His steps follow the story, and the answer fits the beads on the table.
beats.redirect: The beads on the table do not match his answer, so Joaquín checks which step should come first.

beats.lead: A customer asks how Fatima knows the count in the notebook is right.
beats.success: Fatima checks with an estimate and explains why her answer is reasonable.
beats.redirect: The estimate and the answer are far apart, so Fatima looks for the step where the mistake happened.

story.ending: The booth runs all afternoon, and Fatima can explain how each equation matches a story.

panels.says: We have 3 boxes with 7 beads in each box, and 4 beads fall on the floor.
I will write 7 − 4 = 3, and then 3 × 3.
The 4 beads fell out of all the beads, not out of one box. What do we find first?
The total! 3 × 7 = 21, and then 21 − 4 = n.

predict.q: Before Joaquín solves it, predict how many beads are left on the table.
predict.why: The total is 3 × 7 = 21 beads, and 4 fall, so 21 − 4 = 17 beads are left.

transfer.relationship: A total made from equal groups, and then changed by taking some away
phrasings: 5 bags with 8 beads in each bag, and then 13 beads are used
First 5 × 8 = 40, and then 40 − 13 = n
A tape diagram of 5 groups of 8 with a piece of 13 removed

decoys.why: This adds the number of bags to the beads in a bag. It does not join 5 equal groups of 8.
This adds 13 beads to the total, but in the story 13 beads are used up and taken away.

modeling.title: Planning bracelets at the booth
modeling.scenario: A fictional school fair booth makes bracelets from bags of beads. All the numbers are invented for the exercise.
assumptions: Every bag holds the same number of beads.
Every bracelet uses the same number of beads.
No other beads are used, broken or lost.
prompts: How many beads does the booth have in all?
How many bracelets can the booth make if each bracelet uses 6 beads?
If 6 beads get lost, how many beads are left and how many bracelets can the booth still make?
limits: Real bags might hold slightly different numbers of beads.
Real beads can break or roll away, so the count can change.

sentence.base: The unknown number in the equation is 27.
sentence.because: The unknown number in the equation is 27 because 5 × 8 = 40 and 40 − 13 = 27.
sentence.but: The booth began with 40 beads, but the unknown number is 27 after the bracelets.
sentence.so: The equation 5 × 8 − 13 = n matches the story, so the unknown n is 27.

diagnostic.prompt: Read this story: 3 boxes have 9 crayons in each box, and 7 crayons break. Write an equation with a letter for the unknown and solve it. Tell how you know your answer is reasonable.
lookFor: Finds the total first, 3 × 9 = 27
Writes an equation such as 27 − 7 = n or 3 × 9 − 7 = n with a letter
Checks with an estimate or by adding back that 20 makes sense
diagnostic.language: Let the student act out the story with counters before writing any equation. If the counters show 20 left, the barrier is turning the story into symbols, not the arithmetic.

extension.task: Write your own two-step story that uses 4 × 6 and then adds 5 more. Write an equation with a letter for the unknown and solve it.
extension.reasoning: Explain why your equation uses multiplication first and then addition.

en.learning: Your child is learning to write equations for stories that take two steps, using a letter for the number we do not know.
en.say: Say "What do we know? What do we not know? What happens first?" before you write any numbers.
en.ask: We have 3 packs of 6 pencils and give away 4. How many pencils are left, and what are the two steps?
en.activity: Make up a store story with your child using real items, like 4 boxes of 5 crackers and 3 eaten. Write the equation together with a letter for the unknown.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo a escribir ecuaciones para problemas de dos pasos, usando una letra para el número que no conocemos.
es.say: Digan "¿Qué sabemos? ¿Qué no sabemos? ¿Qué pasa primero?" antes de escribir los números.
es.ask: Tenemos 3 paquetes de 6 lápices y regalamos 4. ¿Cuántos lápices quedan y cuáles son los dos pasos?
es.activity: Inventen un cuento de tienda con su hijo o hija usando cosas reales, como 4 cajas de 5 galletas y 3 galletas comidas. Escriban juntos la ecuación con una letra para el número desconocido.

skills.objective: Students compare strategies for multiplying, including breaking apart a factor with the distributive property and multiplying a one-digit number by a multiple of 10, and they explain why different strategies give the same product.
skills.studentObjective: I can solve a multiplication problem in more than one way and explain why the answers match.
skills.languageObjective: I will compare two strategies using because, but and so with the words strategy, break apart, distributive property and efficient.
successCriteria: I break apart a factor into two easier numbers and multiply each part.
I add the partial products to find the whole product.
I multiply a one-digit number by a multiple of 10 and say how many tens I have.
I explain why two strategies reach the same product and which one I prefer.
skills.bigIdea: A multiplication fact can be split into easier facts that add back together, and different strategies for the same problem must give the same product.

syntax: I break apart ___ into ___ and ___, so ___ × ___ = ___ + ___.
Both strategies work because ___, but I prefer ___ since ___.
discourse: Compare two strategies and say what each one depends on
Justify a preference with a reason about the numbers

domains.listening: Students listen to a speaker break apart a number and tell which two products are added.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner how they split a factor and why the parts add back to the whole.
domains.reading: Students read a short passage and mark the numbers each student uses for the same problem.
domains.writing: Students write a sentence that compares two strategies and gives a reason for choosing one.

vocab.def: A plan or method you choose to solve a problem.
vocab.example: Break apart 7 into 5 and 2 to find 6 × 7.
vocab.nonExample: A guess that has no plan
vocab.sentence: Ravi uses a different strategy from Samira.

vocab.def: The rule that you can split a factor, multiply each part, and add the products.
vocab.nonExample: 6 × 7 = 6 × 5 + 2, where the 2 is not multiplied
vocab.sentence: The distributive property turns one hard fact into two easy facts.
vocab.morphology: distribute means to give out to each part

vocab.def: To split a number into two smaller numbers that add to make it.
vocab.example: Break apart 7 into 5 and 2.
vocab.nonExample: Throw away part of the 7
vocab.sentence: Samira can break apart 7 into 5 and 2.

vocab.def: A number you get by counting by tens, like 10, 20, 30 or 40.
vocab.example: 30 is 3 tens, so it is a multiple of 10.
vocab.nonExample: 35, because it is not 3 tens or 4 tens
vocab.sentence: To find 4 × 30, think of 4 groups of a multiple of 10.

vocab.def: Done in a way that is quick and uses few steps.
vocab.example: A strategy that uses facts you already know well
vocab.nonExample: A strategy that takes many long steps for a small problem
vocab.sentence: Each student picks the strategy that feels efficient for them.
vocab.morphology: from Latin efficere, meaning to bring about

misconceptions.belief: When one factor is broken apart, only the first part needs to be multiplied. The other part can just be added.
misconceptions.why: Students multiply the first piece and then add the second piece, forgetting that both pieces are groups that need the same multiplier.
misconceptions.fix: Draw an area model with the factor split into two sections. Label each section with its own product before adding.

errorCase.story: Kai breaks apart 6 into 5 and 1 to find 7 × 6.
steps: I break apart 6 into 5 and 1.
errorCase.explain: The 1 also means 7 groups of 1. Multiply both parts: 7 × 1 = 7. Then 35 + 7 = 42.

misconceptions.belief: To multiply by a multiple of 10, multiply the digits and leave the answer as it is.
misconceptions.why: Students use the fact for the digit and forget that the groups are tens, so the answer is tens too.
misconceptions.fix: Say the number of tens aloud. Show 4 × 3 tens with place value blocks, and count how many tens there are in all.

errorCase.story: Mina finds 4 × 30.
steps: 30 is 3 tens, and 4 × 3 = 12.
errorCase.explain: 4 × 3 tens is 12 tens, not 12 ones. 12 tens is 120, so 4 × 30 = 120.

misconceptions.belief: If two strategies look different, they must give different products.
misconceptions.why: Students see different steps and expect different results, without noticing that every correct strategy describes the same amount.
misconceptions.fix: Solve the same problem two ways and compare the products side by side. Ask what stayed the same in the picture.

misconceptions.belief: Break apart means that the parts are taken away from each other.
misconceptions.why: In everyday speech, a break is a loss or a gap, so students think the pieces are removed instead of added back together.
misconceptions.fix: Break a stick of linking cubes into two pieces and snap them back together. Say that broken apart pieces are added to make the whole again.

errorCase.story: Tess breaks apart 8 into 5 and 3 to find 8 × 6.
steps: 8 is 5 and 3, so 8 × 6 uses 5 × 6 and 3 × 6.
I take 18 away from 30: 30 − 18 = 12.
errorCase.explain: The parts of 8 join to make 8, so the partial products join too. Add them: 30 + 18 = 48, and 8 × 6 = 48.

reading.title: Chairs for the Concert
reading.text: Samira and Ravi set up chairs for the school concert. There are 6 rows, and each row needs 7 chairs. Samira uses the distributive property. She breaks apart 7 into 5 and 2. She finds 6 × 5 = 30 and 6 × 2 = 12, and then she adds 30 + 12 = 42. Ravi uses a different strategy. He knows that 6 × 6 = 36, and he adds one more row of 6 to get 42. Both strategies give 42 chairs. Samira says her way is more efficient for her, because she knows the facts for 5 and 2 well. Ravi says his way is more efficient for him, because he remembers 6 × 6. A good strategy is correct, and you can explain why it works.
reading.simple: Samira and Ravi set up chairs for a concert. There are 6 rows. Each row has 7 chairs. Samira uses the distributive property. She breaks apart 7 into 5 and 2. She finds 6 × 5 = 30 and 6 × 2 = 12. Then she adds 30 + 12 = 42. Ravi uses a different strategy. He knows 6 × 6 = 36. He adds one more row of 6 to get 42. Both strategies give 42 chairs. A good strategy is correct, and you can explain it.

questions.q: How many chairs are in each row?
questions.a: 7 chairs

questions.q: Why can Samira and Ravi both be right when they use different strategies?
questions.a: Both strategies find the number of chairs in 6 rows of 7, so they must give the same product, 42.

questions.q: How does Samira's break apart strategy get 42?
questions.a: She breaks 7 into 5 and 2, finds 6 × 5 = 30 and 6 × 2 = 12, and adds 30 + 12 = 42.

noticeWonder.prompt: Look at a rectangle of chairs with 6 rows and 7 columns, split into a part with 5 columns and a part with 2 columns. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: A multiplication fact can be found by splitting one factor into two smaller numbers and adding the two partial products.
asn.why: The two parts add back to the factor, so the two groups of products add back to the whole product.

asn.claim: The strategy that is fastest for one student is the fastest for every student.
asn.why: Samira is quick with facts for 5 and 2, while Ravi remembers 6 × 6, so different strategies feel quick to different students.

wyr.q: Would you rather find 6 × 7 by breaking apart 7 into 5 and 2, or by starting from the fact 6 × 6?

compare.b: Ravi finds 6 × 7 with 6 × 6 = 36 and one more 6, so 36 + 6 = 42.
compare.prompt: Both strategies give 42. Which would you choose, and which facts does each one depend on?

debate.claim: Breaking numbers apart makes multiplication harder.
debate.forEvidence: Breaking apart makes more steps, like two products and an addition.
debate.againstEvidence: Each small product is a fact you already know, so the steps are easier even when there are more of them.

listening.script: Listen to Ravi explain his plan for 3 times 15. I break apart 15 into 10 and 5. Three times 10 is 30, and three times 5 is 15. Then I add 30 plus 15, and the product is 45. My cousin says to take 15 away from 30 and get 15. But when you break a number apart, the pieces go back together, so I add the pieces. Ten is a multiple of 10, so three times 10 is 3 tens, which is 30.

tasks.q: What product does Ravi find for 3 times 15?
Ravi's cousin takes 15 away from 30. What is the mistake?
options: Partial products are added, not subtracted.
He should have multiplied 30 and 15.
He broke apart the wrong number.
tasks.why: The pieces of 15 go back together, so the partial products are added: 30 + 15 = 45.

story.title: Setting Up the Concert
story.goal: set up all the concert chairs quickly and correctly
story.intro: Samira and Ravi are in charge of the chairs for the school concert. The music teacher wants to know how many chairs are in each section before the doors open.

beats.lead: Samira looks at the first section and decides how to break apart the numbers.
beats.success: She splits a factor into two easier numbers, and the first section is counted quickly.
beats.redirect: The count is too small, so Samira checks whether she multiplied both parts.

beats.lead: Ravi counts the second section a different way and compares his answer with Samira's.
beats.success: Both answers match, and the students explain why different strategies agree.
beats.redirect: The answers do not match, so they line up their steps to find the first one that is different.

beats.lead: The music teacher asks which strategy was most efficient for the big back section.
beats.success: Samira and Ravi each give a reason that uses the numbers, and the teacher picks a plan.
beats.redirect: The reasons do not mention the numbers, so the students add the facts that each strategy uses.

story.ending: The auditorium is ready, and Samira and Ravi can explain several ways to find the same total.

panels.says: We need 5 rows of 40 chairs for the lawn.
What is 5 × 4?
That is 20. So the answer is 20 chairs.
Forty is 4 tens, so 5 × 4 tens is 20 what?
Oh! It is 20 tens, which is 200 chairs.

predict.q: Before Ravi fixes his answer, predict the product of 5 × 40.
predict.why: 5 × 4 tens is 20 tens, and 20 tens is 200.

transfer.relationship: A product can be found by splitting a factor into parts, multiplying each part, and adding the results
phrasings: 6 rows of 7 chairs split into 6 rows of 5 and 6 rows of 2
30 chairs and 12 chairs make 42 chairs
An area model with 6 rows split into a part with 5 columns and a part with 2 columns

decoys.why: The parts of 7 are added, not subtracted. This gives 18, not 42.
Only the 5 is multiplied by 6, so this leaves out 6 × 2 and gives 32, not 42.

modeling.title: Setting up concert chairs
modeling.scenario: A fictional school sets up chairs in two sections for a concert. All the numbers are invented for the exercise.
assumptions: Every row has the same number of chairs.
The side section uses the same number of chairs in each row as the main section.
No chair is added or taken away.
prompts: Use a break apart strategy to find how many chairs are in the main section.
How many chairs are in the side section?
How many chairs are there in both sections, and how could you check with a different strategy?
limits: Real rooms have aisles, so rows might not all be the same length.
Real concerts may add extra chairs at the last minute.

sentence.because: The distributive property helps find 6 × 7 = 42 because 6 × 5 plus 6 × 2 equals 30 plus 12.
sentence.but: The distributive property uses more steps, but each step is an easy fact.
sentence.so: Breaking apart 7 into 5 and 2 gives two easy products, so the strategy finds 42.

diagnostic.prompt: Find 7 × 8 by breaking apart one factor. Draw an area model, write the two partial products, and add them. Then solve it a second way.
lookFor: Splits one factor, such as 8 into 5 and 3, and keeps the other factor the same
Writes 7 × 5 = 35 and 7 × 3 = 21 and adds to get 56
Checks with a second strategy, such as 7 × 7 = 49 and one more 7
diagnostic.language: Let the student cut a paper rectangle into two parts and label the partial products before explaining. If the area model is right, the barrier is the strategy vocabulary, not the facts.

extension.task: Find 6 × 40, 6 × 4 and 6 × 44. Show how the first two products help find the third.
extension.reasoning: Explain how you know that 6 × 44 is the sum of two products.

en.learning: Your child is learning to break apart a multiplication problem into easier pieces and to compare different ways of solving it.
en.say: Say "Split one number into two easy parts, multiply each part, then add." Ask your child why it works.
en.ask: How could you find 4 × 12 by thinking about 4 × 10 and 4 × 2?
en.activity: Set out 6 rows of 7 coins. Cover part of the rows to show 6 × 5 and 6 × 2, add the two parts, and compare with counting every coin.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo a separar un problema de multiplicación en partes más fáciles y a comparar distintas maneras de resolverlo.
es.say: Digan "Separen un número en dos partes fáciles, multipliquen cada parte y luego sumen". Pregunten a su hijo o hija por qué funciona.
es.activity: Pongan 6 filas de 7 monedas. Tapen una parte para mostrar 6 × 5 y 6 × 2, sumen las dos partes y comparen con contar todas las monedas.

skills.objective: Students use the relationship between multiplication and division to build fact families, find an unknown factor in an equation, and fluently divide within 100 by thinking of a multiplication fact.
skills.studentObjective: I can use a multiplication fact to solve a division fact and find a missing factor.
skills.languageObjective: I will explain how multiplication and division are connected using because, but and so with the words fact family, inverse operations, unknown factor and quotient.
successCriteria: I write all four facts in a fact family for three numbers.
I find an unknown factor by dividing the product by the factor I know.
I check a division answer by multiplying the quotient by the divisor.
I tell whether a number in a story is the number of groups or the size of each group.
skills.bigIdea: Multiplication and division use the same three numbers in a fact family, and each operation undoes the other.

syntax: Division undoes multiplication, so I can check by ___.
discourse: Explain how one multiplication fact gives other facts
Justify a division answer by multiplying

domains.listening: Students listen to a fact family and tell which fact does not belong.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner the four facts in a fact family and say how they are connected.
domains.reading: Students read a short passage and underline the three numbers that make a fact family.
domains.writing: Students write a sentence that explains how a multiplication fact checks a division fact.

vocab.def: A set of multiplication and division facts that use the same three numbers.
vocab.nonExample: 7 × 8 = 56 and 7 + 8 = 15, because they use different numbers
vocab.sentence: The numbers 7, 8 and 56 make a fact family.

vocab.def: Two operations where one undoes the other, such as multiplication and division.
vocab.nonExample: Adding 8 and then adding 8 again, because the second step does not undo the first
vocab.sentence: Division is the inverse operation of multiplication.
vocab.morphology: inverse comes from a Latin word meaning turned around

vocab.def: The missing number in a multiplication equation when the product and one factor are known.
vocab.example: In □ × 8 = 56, the unknown factor is 7.
vocab.nonExample: The product 56, which is already known
vocab.sentence: Divide the product by the known factor to find the unknown factor.

vocab.def: The answer to a division problem.
vocab.example: In 56 ÷ 8 = 7, the quotient is 7.
vocab.nonExample: The number 56, which is the amount being divided
vocab.sentence: The quotient tells how many groups or how many are in each group.
vocab.morphology: from Latin quotiens, meaning how many times

vocab.def: The answer to a multiplication problem.
vocab.example: In 7 × 8 = 56, the product is 56.
vocab.nonExample: The number 7, which is a factor
vocab.sentence: The product of 7 and 8 is 56.
vocab.everyday: An item for sale in a store

misconceptions.belief: Both division facts in a fact family have the same quotient.
misconceptions.why: Students repeat the first quotient they found, or they match the answer to the last number they saw, without checking by multiplying.
misconceptions.fix: For each division fact, say the multiplication fact that checks it. The quotient is the missing factor, and the two missing factors are different numbers.

errorCase.story: Dev writes the fact family for 4, 6 and 24.
errorCase.explain: 24 ÷ 6 = 4, because 6 × 4 = 24. The two division facts give 6 and 4, one for each factor.

misconceptions.belief: To find an unknown factor, multiply the product by the factor you know.
misconceptions.why: Students see a multiplication sign in the equation and multiply the two numbers they can see.
misconceptions.fix: Say the equation as a question: some number of 7s makes 56. Then use division to find how many sevens fit in 56 and check by multiplying.

errorCase.story: Lena solves the equation k × 7 = 56.
steps: The equation is k × 7 = 56.
I multiply 56 × 7 to find k.
errorCase.explain: The product, 56, is known and a factor is missing, so divide: 56 ÷ 7 = 8. Check it: 8 × 7 = 56.

misconceptions.belief: The answer to a division problem always tells how many are in each group.
misconceptions.why: Students first meet division as sharing, so they read every quotient as a share instead of looking at what the story already tells.
misconceptions.fix: Label every number in the story as the total, the number of groups or the size of each group, and then say what the quotient counts.

errorCase.story: Tomás packs 20 apples with 4 apples in each bag.
steps: So there are 5 apples in each bag.
errorCase.explain: The story already says 4 apples are in each bag. The 5 tells how many bags Tomás fills, and 5 × 4 = 20 checks it.

misconceptions.belief: The inverse of a number or an operation means writing it backward, so the inverse of 24 is 42.
misconceptions.why: In everyday language, inverse and reverse can sound alike, so students think they should flip the numbers around.
misconceptions.fix: Say that an inverse operation undoes what the first one did, like unzipping undoes zipping. Use real objects to build 7 groups of 8 and then undo them into 8 in each group.

reading.title: Oranges at the Market
reading.text: Chidi and Hana sell oranges at a market stand. They pack the oranges into 7 crates, and each crate holds 8 oranges. They write 7 × 8 = 56. The product is 56. Hana says that 7, 8 and 56 make a fact family, because the numbers are related by multiplication and division. The family has four facts: 7 × 8 = 56, 8 × 7 = 56, 56 ÷ 7 = 8 and 56 ÷ 8 = 7. Then Chidi thinks about 56 ÷ 8. He asks, 8 times what number is 56? That number is the unknown factor, and it is 7, so the quotient is 7. Multiplication and division are inverse operations, because one undoes the other.
reading.simple: Chidi and Hana sell oranges. They pack 7 crates. Each crate holds 8 oranges. They write 7 × 8 = 56. The product is 56. Hana says 7, 8 and 56 make a fact family. The family has four facts: 7 × 8 = 56, 8 × 7 = 56, 56 ÷ 7 = 8 and 56 ÷ 8 = 7. Chidi asks, 8 times what number is 56? That number is the unknown factor. It is 7, so the quotient is 7. Multiplication and division are inverse operations. One undoes the other.

questions.q: How many oranges are in each crate?
questions.a: 8 oranges

questions.q: Why does Chidi think about 8 times what number to solve 56 ÷ 8?
questions.a: Division undoes multiplication, so the missing factor in 8 × □ = 56 is the answer to 56 ÷ 8.

questions.q: Write the two division facts in the fact family for 7, 8 and 56.

wdntb.why: The first three facts are true and belong to one fact family, but 56 ÷ 8 is 7, not 8.

noticeWonder.prompt: Look at an array with 7 rows and 8 columns and the four number sentences written beside it. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: If you know that 7 × 8 = 56, you also know two division facts.
asn.why: The same three numbers give 56 ÷ 7 = 8 and 56 ÷ 8 = 7.

asn.claim: A fact family has four different equations.
asn.why: 7 × 8 gives four different equations, but 7 × 7 = 49 gives only two, 7 × 7 = 49 and 49 ÷ 7 = 7.

wyr.q: Would you rather find 56 ÷ 8 by asking 8 times what is 56, or by drawing 56 oranges in groups of 8?

compare.a: Ana finds 42 ÷ 6 by asking 6 times what number is 42, and she gets 7.
compare.b: Ben finds 42 ÷ 6 by subtracting 6 again and again until he reaches 0, and he counts 7 subtractions.
compare.prompt: Why do both strategies find 7? Which one uses the inverse operation?

debate.claim: Knowing multiplication facts makes division easy.
debate.forEvidence: Every division fact is a multiplication fact with a missing factor, like 56 ÷ 8 = 7 because 8 × 7 = 56.
debate.againstEvidence: A student can know 8 × 7 = 56 and still not see that 56 ÷ 8 asks for the missing factor, so the connection must be learned too.

listening.script: Listen to Hana explain a fact family. I have 6, 9 and 54. Six times 9 is 54, and 9 times 6 is 54. Fifty-four divided by 6 is 9, and 54 divided by 9 is 6. My friend says that 54 divided by 9 is 9, because he wrote the first answer again. But I check. Nine times 9 is 81, not 54. The unknown factor must be 6, because 9 times 6 is 54. Multiplication helps me check division.

tasks.q: What is 54 divided by 9?
tasks.why: 9 × 6 = 54, so the quotient of 54 ÷ 9 is 6.

tasks.q: Hana's friend says that 54 divided by 9 is 9. How does Hana show that this is wrong?
options: She multiplies 9 by 9 and gets 81, not 54.
She adds 9 and 9 and gets 18.
She counts by fives up to 54.
tasks.why: If the quotient were 9, then 9 × 9 would equal 54, but 9 × 9 = 81.

story.title: Packing at the Market
story.goal: pack and share the fruit by using fact families
story.intro: Hana and Chidi help at a fruit stand in the neighborhood market. Crates, bags and boxes are stacked everywhere, and every customer wants the fruit packed in equal amounts.

beats.lead: Hana packs the first crates and writes a multiplication fact for what she packed.
beats.success: She uses the same three numbers to write two division facts, and the crates match her plan.
beats.redirect: The crates do not match, so Hana checks each division fact by multiplying.

beats.lead: Chidi finds an order with one factor missing and has to decide how to find it.
beats.success: He divides the product by the factor he knows and checks by multiplying.
beats.redirect: His answer does not check, so Chidi asks what number times the known factor makes the product.

beats.lead: A customer asks whether the number in the answer is the number of bags or the number in each bag.
beats.success: Hana labels each number in the story and explains what the quotient counts.
beats.redirect: The label does not fit the story, so Hana rereads it and names the total first.

story.ending: The stand is packed and neat, and Hana can show how multiplication and division work together.

panels.says: I need to find 72 ÷ 9, and I do not know it.
What do you know about 9 and 72?
I could multiply 72 × 9.
That goes the wrong way. Division asks, 9 times what number is 72?

predict.q: Before Chidi finishes, predict the quotient of 72 ÷ 9.

transfer.relationship: Three numbers linked by multiplication and division: two factors and their product
phrasings: 7 crates with 8 oranges in each crate make 56 oranges
8 times what number is 56?
56 oranges packed 8 to a crate fill 7 crates

decoys.why: This is a fact family for addition and subtraction. It uses different numbers and a different relationship.
Subtracting 8 once is not division. It leaves 48, not 7.

modeling.title: Packing fruit at the market
modeling.scenario: A fictional market stand packs fruit into bags and boxes of equal size. All the numbers are invented for the exercise.
assumptions: Every bag holds exactly 9 oranges.
Every box holds exactly 5 pears.
No fruit is left out or bruised.
prompts: How many bags do the 72 oranges fill?
Write the fact family for 8, 9 and 72.
Write a multiplication equation with an unknown factor for the pears, and tell how many boxes they fill.
limits: Real fruit comes in different sizes, so bags may not hold exactly the same number.
Some fruit may be bruised and left out, so the counts could change.

sentence.base: The numbers 7, 8 and 56 make a fact family.
sentence.because: The numbers 7, 8 and 56 make a fact family because 7 × 8 = 56 and 56 ÷ 8 = 7.
sentence.but: Multiplication finds the product of 7 and 8, but division finds a missing factor from 56.
sentence.so: Division undoes multiplication, so 7 × 8 = 56 means that 56 ÷ 8 = 7.

diagnostic.prompt: Write the four facts in the fact family for 5, 9 and 45. Then solve 9 × □ = 45 by using one of the division facts.
lookFor: Chooses 45 ÷ 9 and finds the unknown factor 5
Says that the unknown factor is found by dividing the product by the known factor
diagnostic.language: Let the student build 9 groups with counters and undo them into equal groups before writing. If the counters show the right groups, the barrier is the fact family language, not the operations.

extension.task: Write one story that matches 36 ÷ 4 = 9 and a different story that matches 36 ÷ 9 = 4.
extension.reasoning: Explain why both stories use the same three numbers but ask different questions.

en.learning: Your child is learning that multiplication and division are connected, so a multiplication fact helps solve a division fact.
en.say: Say "If 7 groups of 8 make 56, then 56 split into groups of 8 makes 7 groups."
en.activity: Use 24 buttons. Make equal groups of 4, then equal groups of 6, and write the multiplication and division sentences you find.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo que la multiplicación y la división están conectadas, así que un hecho de multiplicación ayuda a resolver un hecho de división.
es.say: Digan "Si 7 grupos de 8 hacen 56, entonces 56 repartido en grupos de 8 hace 7 grupos".
es.activity: Usen 24 botones. Hagan grupos iguales de 4 y luego de 6, y escriban las oraciones de multiplicación y de división que encuentren.
